components.quote: FDCPA should define what constitutes reasonable period of time.
In my experience most attorneys who represent a debtor do not return communication inquiries about representation.
In most cases the delay in response may be caused by the debtor paying installment payments to the attorney to file a bankruptcy proceeding.
When the debtor does not keep the repayment terms a creditor is presently not notified that the representation has terminated  and there is no attorney representation.

Debt collectors should not be allowed to alter their caller ID information.
They call misrepresenting themselves as "Process Servers" inquiring information about another person's debt.
This prevents the consumer from reporting the debt collector for violating consumer protection laws because a false identify was used.

I am concerned about the perception consumers have concerning older debts.
Many consumers appear to be under the impression, if they haven't managed to pay off the debt within the first initial years, they should *ignore* it until it falls off their credit report.
Reviving the debt is the issue.
they might be in much better financial standing now.
They're concerned about how paying a debt affects their credit score.
If a debt is outstanding, and repying part (or all) of this debt actually would *worsen* a consumer's credit, it seems counter-intuitive.
It works both against the interests of creditors and debt collectors - and the interest of consumers who owe money on a debt.
this is a concern which should be addressed.

Everyone works at different times.
